message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to very different lineages:

| Taxonomic level | Lion | Zebra |
|-----------------|------|-------|
| Order | Carnivora (Feliformia) | Perissodactyla |
| Superorder | Laurasiatheria | Laurasiatheria |
| Class | Mammalia | Mammalia |

Because they diverge at the order level, their most recent common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the two orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor was a **Laurasiatherian placental mammal** that lived roughly **90–100 million years ago** during the Late Cretaceous. In other words, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is a relatively ancient mammal that gave rise to the entire Laurasiatherian clade, which later split into the odd‑toed ungulates (Perissodactyla) and the carnivores (Carnivora).

The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want a biological answer. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be a common ancestor in the mammalian lineage. Both are mammals, but lions are felids (family Felidae), zebras are equids (family Equidae). They diverged from a common ancestor in the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla? Actually lions are in order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in order Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates). So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps a placental mammal ancestor. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is the eutherian ancestor. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: that would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both orders, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a mammalian ancestor that lived about 90-100 million years ago. But maybe the answer: "The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived around 90 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of all placental mammals" if we go further back. But the question likely expects: "The common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the order Carnivora and the order Perissodactyla, which is a Laurasiatherian mammal that lived about 90 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of all mammals" if they want a simpler answer. But the question: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" Might be answered: "They share a common ancestor that is a placental mammal that lived about 90 million years ago, belonging to the Laurasiatheria clade." Or "the last common ancestor of the two species is the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae, which is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla."
